newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Oil prices bounce as Iraq dithers on exports.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Oil prices bounce as Iraq dithers on exports.

text.p: World oil prices bounced on Friday as concern persisted about a delay in the resumption of Iraqi crude exports under the terms of a United Nations humanitarian agreement.

Baghdad's U.N. envoy Nizar Hamdoon said Iraq had no interest in delaying the limited sales, permitted under the terms of an oil-for-food deal implemented last December, but wanted assurances on U.N. plans to distribute food and medicine bought with the proceeds.

Oil prices began the week falling to a new 13-month low but the possibility of a delay in supplies from Iraq, which averaged about 660,000 barrels per day (bpd) over the first six months of the accord, sparked a reversal.
London July futures for Benchmark Brent Blend crude were trading 34 cents up on the day at $17.78 by 1638 GMT.

Worries that political posturing by Iraq might delay the deal were heightened when the United Nations on Thursday said a team of its weapons inspectors had been blocked from entering three suspected military sites.
"It is difficult to evaluate the reasoning behind Baghdad's tactics at the moment, but in any case the market will react positively to the news," brokers GNI said in a report.
The U.N. Security Council last week extended the oil-for-food deal for another six months from June 8, allowing Baghdad to sell a further $2 billion worth of crude oil.
European oil traders are not expecting shipments to resume until July at the earliest.
Market sentiment was nervous with investment funds, among the most aggressive sellers early in the week, eager to recover some protection against a rebound.
With the threat of supply from Iraq being delayed market players were keen not to be left out of a rally.
"It only takes one headline for people to buy at the moment," one dealer said.
Fund-led buying kicked in to drive prices higher with market players scrambling to cover their positions before they were obliged to settle expiring futures and options contracts.

The expiry of the July Brent futures contract at the close of business on Friday lifted demand but brokers said a bigger driving force came from speculators rooting around for paper to satisfy the expiry of the prompt options contract on the New York market.
And initial figures indicating that supply of oil from the North Sea might be thiner than expected also helped support prices.
The first of Norway's July loading programmes showed the Gullfaks system loading 21 cargoes, down three from June. Only a small increase in Brent loadings was reported.
The recent price slump was also refocussing attention on rampant quota violations by several OPEC producers just 10 days before the cartel's ministers meet in Vienna.
While a handful of Gulf producers led by Saudi Arabia maintain spare capacity and output discipline, others like Venezuela and Nigeria are pumping at full steam without regard for oil prices.
"I think there will be some stress on the need to adhere to quotas," said a Gulf source familiar with Saudi oil policy.
But observers dismiss any real hope of the quota violators, buoyed by foreign oil company investors, reining in output.
"Zero chance," said one OPEC national company executive.
